sections.title: 3 or 4 Positions of a Dice
sections.content: When 3 or 4 different views of the same dice are given, you do not need to use all of them. Step 1: Select any two favorable views that show at least one or two common faces. Step 2: Identify the common face(s). Step 3: Compare the changing faces. Step 4: Use elimination to determine the opposite face.

sections.title: Using Two Common Faces (Advanced Rule)
sections.content: If two views have two common faces in the same relative position, then the third face that changes in both views will be opposite. Step 1: Identify the two common faces. Step 2: Observe the third face in both views. Step 3: The changing faces are opposite to each other.

sections.title: Using One Common Face (Extended Logic)
sections.content: If only one face is common in two views, then all other visible faces in those views are adjacent to that common face. Step 1: Note the common face. Step 2: List all faces appearing with it. Step 3: The face not appearing with it will be opposite.

sections.title: Textual Open Dice (Net Concept)
sections.content: In open dice questions, the cube is unfolded in a cross or similar shape. Step 1: Identify the center face. Step 2: The four faces around the center are adjacent to it. Step 3: The face attached externally folds opposite to the center. Step 4: Use alternate face logic to identify other opposite pairs.

sections.title: Alternate Face Rule in Nets
sections.content: In a straight line of three faces in a net (A-B-C), A and C become opposite after folding. This rule works especially in cross-shaped nets.

sections.title: Dice with Letters or Symbols
sections.content: Numbers may be replaced with letters (A, B, C) or symbols (@, #, $). The logic remains the same. Step 1: Identify common symbol(s). Step 2: Note adjacent symbols. Step 3: Use elimination to find the opposite symbol.

sections.title: Example: Open Dice Problem
sections.content: Given: 1 is at center, 2 top, 3 bottom, 4 left, 5 right, and 6 attached above 2. Step 1: 2, 3, 4, 5 are adjacent to 1. Step 2: 6 folds opposite to 1. Step 3: 4 and 5 become opposite. Therefore, 4 is opposite to 5.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Trying to combine all 3 or 4 views unnecessarily. 2. Confusing rotation with reflection. 3. Ignoring alternate face rule in nets. 4. Forgetting that opposite faces never appear together.

tricks.title: Pick the Best Two Views
tricks.explanation: From 3 or 4 views, choose two that clearly show one or two common faces.
tricks.example: If 3 is on top in two views, compare only those two.

tricks.title: Two Common Faces Shortcut
tricks.explanation: If two faces are common in two views, the third changing faces are opposite.
tricks.example: 2 and 3 are common; 4 changes to 5. So 4 and 5 are opposite.

tricks.title: One Common Face Elimination
tricks.explanation: List all faces appearing with the common face. The remaining unseen face is opposite.
tricks.example: If 1 appears with 2, 3, 4, 5, then 6 is opposite to 1.

tricks.title: Alternate Line Net Trick
tricks.explanation: In a straight sequence A-B-C in a net, A and C are opposite after folding.
tricks.example: If 1-2-6 are in a line, 1 and 6 are opposite.

tricks.title: Center Face Rule
tricks.explanation: The center face in a net is adjacent to the four surrounding faces.
tricks.example: If 1 is center, 2, 3, 4, 5 are adjacent to it.

tricks.title: Symbol Dice Elimination
tricks.explanation: If a symbol appears with four different symbols, the remaining one is opposite.
tricks.example: @ appears with #, $, %, &; so the last symbol is opposite to @.

tricks.title: Rotation Check Trick
tricks.explanation: Mentally rotate the dice to verify adjacency. Opposite faces cannot become neighbors.
tricks.example: If A is opposite B, they cannot appear side by side in any valid rotation.
